text:
Today I got promoted to Senior Software Engineer.

Three years ago I joined a fintech startup as a mid-level engineer with no payments background. My first month was mostly me staring at reconciliation jobs and asking a lot of questions.

A few things I'm grateful for:

- A team that let me break things in staging before I could break them in prod
- A manager who gave me the hard migrations, even when I doubted I could do them
- Engineers who reviewed my code like they wanted me to get better, not like they wanted to win

Senior is a bigger job than writing good code. It's about making the people around you faster and making sure the next hire doesn't have to learn what I learned the hard way.

Thanks to everyone who took a chance on me. More to come.

After almost six years at Deloitte, I'm leaving to start my own consulting firm.

It's a scary thing to write. I'm proud of the work I did there and the people I worked with. I learned how to run a serious engagement, how to build a deck that survives a steering committee, and how to stay calm when a client is angry at 11pm.

What I didn't learn there is how to build something that's mine. So that's what I'm doing.

The firm will focus on helping mid-sized operations teams cut process waste and actually get the changes to stick. I'll be taking on a small number of clients this year, so if that sounds like your problem, send me a message.

Thanks to my former colleagues, my clients, and my family for putting up with the last few months of me thinking out loud.

Last month I got laid off. I didn't expect to write about it, but a few things surprised me enough that I want to.

1. My identity was more tied to my job title than I realized. For the first week I kept answering 'what do you do?' with my old company's name.

2. Money stress is not the same as financial planning. Once I wrote down actual numbers, the panic shrank to something I could work with.

3. Most of the people who helped me were not the ones I expected. Former colleagues I hadn't talked to in years sent introductions without being asked.

4. I'm more useful when I'm specific about what I want. Vague 'open to anything' messages got me nowhere. A clear note about the role I'm after got three replies in a day.

If you're in the middle of this right now, I'm sorry. It's hard, and it's not a reflection of your worth. If you want to talk through your search, my DMs are open.

Most companies don't get remote work wrong because of tools. They get it wrong because they copy the office and try to make it happen over video.

A few patterns I keep seeing:

They schedule more meetings to replace hallway conversations, then wonder why everyone is exhausted by Thursday.

They write nothing down, because people were 'in the room anyway.' Remote teams that thrive write things down almost obsessively.

They measure presence instead of output. If you're watching green dots, you're managing anxiety, not work.

The companies doing it well treat asynchronous communication as the default and meetings as the exception. They invest in onboarding, because new people can't absorb culture by osmosis. And they make it easy to be offline without it being a career risk.

Remote isn't a perk you hand out. It's a set of habits, and most teams haven't built them yet.

What's one habit your remote team got right?

We're hiring two backend engineers in Berlin.

The stack: Go and Postgres. You'll work on the core services that move money and data for our customers, so reliability matters a lot here.

What we're looking for:
- Solid experience with Go in production
- Real understanding of Postgres: indexes, query plans, migrations that don't lock tables
- A habit of writing clear code and clear tickets
- Comfort with on-call and owning what you ship

What we offer:
- Hybrid work from our Berlin office, with two days a week at home
- A team of 12 engineers who actually review each other's code
- Competitive salary and a generous equity package

If you want to build systems that people depend on, send me a message or apply through the link in the comments.

My first manager taught me the most important leadership lesson I've ever learned, and he did it by accident.

I came to him with a problem I'd been stuck on for two days. Instead of fixing it, he asked me what I had already tried. Then he asked what I thought the next step was. I hated it. I wanted the answer.

But by the end of that conversation I had the answer, and I understood the system better than I had before.

Years later I realized he wasn't being lazy or unhelpful. He was making sure I didn't become dependent on him.

Now when someone brings me a problem, my first question is usually 'what have you tried?' It's slower in the moment. It's almost always faster over a year.

Who taught you something by refusing to just tell you the answer?

We're excited to announce that we've closed a $4M seed round led by Accel.

When we started this company, we were two people with a rough idea and a lot of late nights. Today we have a team of [X] and customers who rely on us every day. This round lets us do more of what's working: deepen the product, hire the people we've been waiting for, and get closer to the customers who need us most.

A big thank you to the Accel team for believing in what we're building, and to our angel investors, advisors, and early customers who took a chance on us before we had much to show.

We're hiring across engineering, product, and go-to-market. If you want to help build this, check out our careers page.

Onward.

AI is changing marketing, but probably not in the way most people are talking about.

The loud version is that AI will replace copywriters and designers. Some tasks will go that way. But the bigger shift is in how fast we can test ideas and how much data we can actually act on.

A few things I've noticed:

The bottleneck has moved. Producing a hundred ad variants used to take a week. Now it takes an afternoon. The hard part is knowing which variant is worth showing and why.

Taste matters more. When everyone can generate competent copy, the brands that stand out are the ones with a clear point of view and the discipline to say no to most of what the tools suggest.

Measurement is getting closer to reality. Better attribution and faster experiments mean marketers can learn in days instead of quarters.

The teams I see doing well treat AI as a fast junior collaborator, not an oracle. They still check the work, and they still talk to customers.

Where are you seeing the biggest change in your marketing work?

Our team just shipped our new mobile app, and I'm proud of every person who made it happen.

It took months of late nights, a lot of rewrites, and more than a few 'are we sure this is the right approach?' conversations. Everyone on the team pushed to make it simple and fast, and it shows.

Thanks to our designers, engineers, QA, and the support team who helped us test on every device we could find.

If you've got the app, I'd love to hear what you think. Feedback is the best part of shipping.

Now on to the next one.

Five things I wish someone had told me when I started as a junior developer:

1. Read other people's code every day. You learn more from a good pull request than from most tutorials.

2. Ask questions early. Being stuck for four hours is not heroic. Ask after 30 minutes with a clear description of what you've tried.

3. Learn your debugger and your logs well. Guessing is slower than looking.

4. Write things down. Notes, comments, and short design docs save your future self and your teammates.

5. Don't measure yourself against senior engineers. Measure yourself against where you were six months ago.

What would you add to this list?

My first startup failed after two years. I'm writing this because I think we talk about failure in a way that makes it sound either glamorous or shameful, and it was neither.

We ran out of money because we grew faster than our revenue, and we didn't say that clearly enough to ourselves for too long. I had the numbers. I didn't want to read them.

There were good parts too. I learned to sell, to hire badly and then better, and to tell a team the truth on a Monday morning when everyone was hoping for good news.

The hardest part was telling the people who had trusted us. Some of them were kind about it. Some were not. I'm grateful for the ones who were kind.

If you're in the middle of something that isn't working, look at the numbers now, not later. And if you've failed at something, I'd like to hear what you learned.

Mental health at work isn't a perk or a wellness campaign. It's a business issue, and most workplaces still treat it like an afterthought.

When people are exhausted, anxious, or afraid to speak up, they make more mistakes, they leave faster, and they stop bringing their best ideas. You can see it in the numbers if you look.

What actually helps, from what I've seen:

Managers who can have an honest conversation about workload without it becoming a performance issue.

Reasonable expectations about response times and after-hours messages.

Access to real support, not just an app with a meditation timer.

Leaders who talk openly about their own limits. It gives everyone else permission to have them too.

If you've had to fix this in your own team, what worked for you?

A customer service experience taught me more about business than any course I've taken.

Last month I called a company about a billing error. I expected a long wait and a script. Instead, the agent listened, said 'you're right, this shouldn't have happened,' fixed it in two minutes, and then told me what they were changing so it wouldn't happen to the next person.

I didn't just forgive the mistake. I told three people about it that week.

A few takeaways:

A mistake handled well can build more trust than a smooth experience that never went wrong.

Empowering frontline staff is not a cost. The agent clearly had permission to solve my problem, and that made all the difference.

Customers remember how you fix things, not just whether they broke.

What's the best service experience you've had recently?

I just finished my MBA at INSEAD, and I want to thank the people who got me here.

To my family, who moved cities with me, covered for me on the weekends I was buried in case studies, and never once asked when I'd be finished. You did more than you know.

To my study group, who argued with me until 2am and made me a better thinker. I won't forget the Tuesday we tried to model a turnaround in a spreadsheet and the file crashed three times.

To the faculty and staff, who pushed us harder than we wanted and reminded us why it mattered.

To my classmates from more than 60 countries, I learned as much from you in the hallways as I did in the classroom.

Now the real work starts. If you're in the job search or thinking about a career change, my inbox is open.

Hustle culture is overrated, and I think it's making us worse at our jobs.

The people I admire most are not the ones who answer messages at midnight. They're the ones who go home at a reasonable time, think clearly, and make good decisions when it matters.

Burnout doesn't show up as a dramatic collapse. It shows up as slower thinking, shorter patience, and a growing list of things you're quietly avoiding.

I'm not against hard work. I'm against confusing busyness with progress. Sometimes the most productive thing you can do is stop, rest, and look at whether you're working on the right thing.

Unpopular opinion, I know. Agree or disagree?

Last year my newsletter hit 10,000 subscribers. I didn't do anything magical, so here's what actually worked.

I wrote every week, even when no one was reading yet. The first year was slow. I wrote for about 40 people, and that was fine.

I picked one specific reader. Not 'marketers,' but 'a marketing manager at a 50-person startup who has to explain the numbers to her CEO.' Every issue got easier to write once I had her in mind.

I shared my own mistakes. The issues that got the most replies were the ones where I admitted I'd gotten something wrong.

I asked readers to forward it to one person. Growth came slowly, then faster, mostly from those forwards.

If you're writing a newsletter, what's holding you back right now?

Networking tips for introverts, from someone who used to dread every event:

1. Go with a goal. 'Meet two people who work in logistics' is much easier than 'network.'

2. Arrive early. The room is quieter and conversations are easier to start.

3. Ask good questions and listen. Most people love talking about their work, and you don't have to be the most charming person in the room.

4. Follow up within 48 hours. A short, specific message beats a long, generic one.

5. Give before you ask. Share an article, make an introduction, or offer a useful answer.

6. Leave when you're done. Two real conversations are worth more than ten shallow ones.

What's worked for you?

Working in sales taught me more about life than I expected.

You learn quickly that rejection isn't personal, even when it feels that way. A 'no' today is usually about timing, budget, or someone else's priorities, not about you.

You learn to listen. The best salespeople I know spend more time asking questions than talking, because the answer is almost always in what the customer tells you.

You learn to be honest about what you can and can't do. Overpromising wins a deal once and loses the relationship for years.

And you learn that consistency beats intensity. Showing up every day, making the calls, and following up matters more than one heroic week.

I still use these lessons in my personal life and in every job since. What's a lesson from your work that followed you everywhere?

Our nonprofit just reached 1,000 volunteers, and I'm still a little stunned.

When we started, we had five people and a shared spreadsheet. Today volunteers run our food pantry, tutor kids after school, and help neighbors with paperwork they'd otherwise struggle with alone.

Every one of those 1,000 people chose to give their time. Some have been with us since the beginning. Some joined last month. All of them made this possible.

Thank you to every volunteer, donor, partner, and family member who showed up. We're not done. There's still a long list of people we want to reach, and we'd love your help.

If you want to get involved, the link to sign up is in the comments.

I returned to work after parental leave this month, and I didn't expect how much I would have to re-learn.

The work was the easy part. Getting back into the rhythm of meetings, Slack, and deadlines took longer than I thought. I also had to figure out how to be a professional again while my brain was still half-asleep from night feeds.

A few things helped:

My manager checked in before I came back, not after I'd already fallen behind.

I blocked my calendar for lunch so I actually ate it.

I let go of the idea that I had to prove I was still as committed as before. I am, just differently.

If you're heading back soon, or you're a manager planning for someone's return, I'd love to hear what helped you.

Quick question for my network: what CRM do you recommend for a small agency of about 8 people?

We currently run everything on spreadsheets and it's getting messy. We need something that handles client contacts, project pipelines, and basic invoicing without requiring a full-time admin to maintain it.

Budget is modest, so I'm looking for something that's affordable and easy for non-technical people to use. Bonus points if it integrates with Google Workspace.

What are you using, and what do you wish you'd known before you picked it? Happy to hear both the wins and the regrets.

Product managers should learn SQL. It's one of the highest-leverage skills you can pick up.

Here's why it matters. Most product questions eventually come down to data. How many users completed onboarding last week? Which feature do retained users actually use? Where do people drop off? If you can answer those questions yourself, you stop waiting in line for an analyst and you make decisions faster.

You don't need to become a data engineer. Learn to write a join, group by a field, and filter by date. That covers most of what you'll need for the first year.

It also makes you a better conversation partner. When you know how the data is structured, you ask better questions, and engineers and analysts take you more seriously.

What's the first query you'd want to run on your product?

Deep Work by Cal Newport changed how I think about my job.

I read it during a stretch where I felt busy all day and got almost nothing meaningful done. My calendar was full, my inbox never reached zero, and I was proud of how responsive I was. The book made me realize responsiveness is not the same as impact.

The idea that stuck with me most is that focused, uninterrupted work on hard problems is becoming rarer and more valuable. So I started blocking two hours in the morning for one important task, turning off notifications, and keeping shallow work for the afternoon.

It didn't fix everything, but the quality of my output went up quickly.

If you've read Deep Work, what did you change because of it? And if you haven't, what's the book that's changed how you work?

Ten years as a nurse. I wanted to write something about it, because people outside the job rarely see what it asks of you.

I've held hands in the hardest moments of people's lives. I've also learned to eat a meal in four minutes, to notice when something is wrong before the monitors do, and to advocate for patients when they're too scared or too tired to do it themselves.

It has made me more patient and less patient at the same time. I have no tolerance for pretending, and endless compassion for people who are frightened.

To the nurses I trained with, the ones who mentored me, and the patients who taught me more than any textbook: thank you.

If you work in healthcare, I'd love to hear what you wish more people understood about your job.

As a recruiter, the biggest mistake I see candidates make in interviews is not preparing questions for the interviewer.

When I ask 'do you have any questions for me?' and the answer is 'no, I think you covered everything,' I lose a bit of confidence. It tells me they either didn't research the role or didn't think about whether this is the right place for them.

Good questions show you're evaluating the company too. Ask about how success is measured in the first six months. Ask what the team's biggest challenge is right now. Ask what the last person in this role did well.

You don't need a perfect question. You just need one that shows you're thinking about the job, not just trying to get it.

What's the best question a candidate has ever asked you?

Next Thursday I'm hosting a free webinar on cloud cost optimization, and I'd love to see you there.

If your cloud bill keeps growing faster than your product, you're not alone. In this session we'll walk through the practical steps teams are using to find waste, right-size resources, and build cost awareness into engineering without slowing anyone down.

You'll leave with:
- A simple way to see where your spend is going
- Three changes you can make the same week
- Answers to your questions from people who have done this in real companies

It's free, and it runs for about 45 minutes. Register through the link in the comments, and feel free to forward it to a colleague who owns your infrastructure budget.

I'm switching careers from teaching to UX design, and I'm more excited than I expected to be.

People sometimes assume teaching doesn't prepare you for design. I disagree. Every lesson I've planned has been a small user research exercise: watching what confuses people, testing a new approach, and adjusting based on what I see. Teachers are already good at empathy and iteration. I just never had the words for it.

The transition hasn't been easy. I've spent evenings learning Figma, rebuilding my portfolio, and getting used to receiving critique on work I care about. But I'm finding my footing.

If you've made a similar move, I'd love to hear how you did it. And if you're hiring junior designers, I'd love to talk.

Learning to say no is one of the most important skills I've built, and it took me far too long.

For years I said yes to everything. New projects, extra meetings, favors that weren't really mine to do. It felt like being a good colleague. In reality, I was spreading myself so thin that the important work suffered.

Saying no doesn't have to be cold. It can sound like this: 'I'd love to help, but I'm focused on the launch this week. Can we look at it next Tuesday?' Or 'That's not something I can take on right now. Have you talked to Sam about it?'

Every no you give is space for a yes that matters more.

What's the hardest thing for you to decline?

Congratulations to my former colleague Priya on her new role as CTO!

I had the privilege of working with Priya for [X] years, and I saw firsthand how she combines deep technical judgment with real care for the people on her team. She has a rare ability to make hard decisions clearly and then bring everyone along.

CTO is a big step, and I have no doubt she'll be excellent at it. The company is lucky to have her.

Priya, I'm proud to have learned from you, and I can't wait to see what you build next.

Congratulations again!

My first year as a freelance designer taught me more about business than design.

A few lessons:

Pricing is part of the craft. I underpriced my first projects because I was afraid to lose them. I learned that clients who respect your rate usually respect your time, too.

Scope creep is constant. Writing clear project briefs and sign-off points saved me more headaches than any design tool.

Discovery is the work that makes the rest easier. The projects that went smoothly were the ones where I spent time understanding the problem before I opened Figma.

You need more than one source of work. Referrals are great, but relying on one client for half your income is risky.

If you're thinking about going freelance, what's the question you most want answered?
